intro: Anscombe asks what makes a bodily movement an intentional action and what gives moral language its force. Her examples connect explanation, agency and judgment without making a person’s preferred description the final word.
description: Elizabeth Anscombe on intention, practical knowledge, double effect and moral obligation, with examples that test action descriptions and justification.

sections.heading: Intention changes what counts as an explanation
paragraphs: Anscombe’s importance begins with a deceptively ordinary question: what are you doing? A person may be moving an arm, operating a pump and supplying a house with water. These descriptions need not pick out three separate performances. They organize one activity differently, and a further answer about the person’s purpose can explain how the descriptions belong together.

The point is not that an invisible feeling turns a neutral movement into an action. An action can be intentional under one description and unintentional under another. Someone may knowingly turn a handle without knowing that the mechanism is making a noise next door. Understanding the action requires attention to the agent’s knowledge and reasons as well as to what happens.

In Intention (1957), this approach reshapes the philosophy of action. In “Modern Moral Philosophy” (1958), Anscombe also presses ethics to clarify action, wanting and human flourishing before relying on sweeping moral theories. Her religious commitments and her criticisms of consequentialism matter to her work, but one can evaluate her analysis of action without first accepting all of her moral conclusions.
listItems: Historical setting: Twentieth-century analytic philosophy supplies debates about mind, language and action. Anscombe’s examples expose assumptions hidden in familiar descriptions.
Signature contribution: Intention belongs to the intelligibility of action under descriptions, not simply to an additional private sensation.
Influence trail: Action theory and renewed interest in virtue inherit questions about practical knowledge and what makes conduct just or unjust.
Signature contribution in use: Knowing that a movement occurred does not yet tell us what the agent was doing it for.
Historical setting and method: Her engagement with Wittgenstein does not make her work a mere commentary; Intention develops its own sustained investigation.
Influence as disagreement: Later readers can retain her questions about agency while rejecting her conclusions about moral law or particular prohibitions.

sections.heading: Knowing what one is doing is not the same as watching it
paragraphs: The relevant question “Why?” asks for a reason for acting, not merely a physiological cause. “To fill the tank” explains pumping differently from a description of muscle contraction. An answer such as “I did not know I was doing that” can show that an action was not intentional under the description being proposed. This does not mean every intentional action follows an elaborate plan or that every sincere explanation is correct.

Practical knowledge is knowledge involved in directing what one does. Anscombe’s shopping-list example contrasts a list guiding a shopper with a detective’s record of the purchases. A mismatch can call for correcting the shopping or correcting the record, depending on the list’s role. The contrast does not make agents infallible: execution may fail, and observation can help them keep an activity on course.

The distinction between an intended means and a foreseen side effect matters to double effect, a form of moral reasoning about actions with good and bad effects. Merely saying “I did not want the harm” does not settle the issue. If harm is the chosen route to the goal, disliking it does not turn it into a side effect. Nor does genuinely unintended harm automatically become permissible; avoidability and the justification for accepting it remain relevant.

Anscombe’s criticism of modern moral language is a further argument. She questions whether a distinctively law-like moral “ought” retains its sense when detached from the law conception that sustained it. This is not the claim that nonbelievers cannot act well. It challenges an account of obligation and proposes renewed attention to concepts such as justice and flourishing.
listItems: Intention: Ask under which description the action is intentional and how the agent’s reasons connect its parts.
Practical knowledge: Knowledge can guide action rather than report it from a spectator’s position. Guidance still permits error and correction.
Modern moral philosophy critique: The law-like use of obligation needs explanation. Its disputed history is not itself proof that secular ethics fails.
Double effect: Distinguish a harmful means from an unwanted consequence; neither the agent’s wording nor the absence of desire for harm settles permissibility.
Historical pressure: Before comparing outcomes, ethical reasoning must identify what is being chosen, by whom and for what purpose.

sections.heading: Can the account justify standards across moral disagreement?
paragraphs: The strongest objection here asks whether virtue and intention can address moral pluralism without importing an unargued authority. Two people may agree completely about what an agent intends and still disagree about whether the action is just. Clarity about intention is therefore necessary for many disputes but insufficient to settle them.

Anscombe has a stronger reply than simply appealing to a vanished lawgiver. “Modern Moral Philosophy” explicitly treats Aristotle as evidence that ethics can be pursued outside a law conception. Concepts such as justice and human flourishing can organize that inquiry. Her challenge is that familiar moral vocabulary should not be allowed to do argumentative work merely through its commanding sound.

The reply leaves a real burden. Which account of flourishing is justified, and how should competing claims about justice be assessed? A critic can also ask whether a concept’s historical origin determines what it can mean now. A secular account of obligation might offer a present justification that does not depend on the genealogy Anscombe disputes. Naming this possibility is not yet a successful account, but it prevents historical diagnosis from being mistaken for a final refutation.

As a hypothetical test, imagine an official falsifying a safety report “to protect jobs.” The benevolent purpose does not erase the deliberate deception, and a useful analysis must include both. It must then ask why the deception is justified or unjustified, rather than treating the explanation of the intention as a moral verdict. The case exposes the gap between making an action intelligible and defending it.
listItems: Best objection: Understanding intentions and invoking virtue do not by themselves establish standards acceptable across deep moral disagreement.
Charitable reply: Anscombe offers an inquiry into justice and flourishing, not a simple claim that ethics is impossible without religious belief.
Contemporary test: In the safety-report case, preserve both the stated aim and the knowingly chosen deception when describing the act.
Charitable reply extended: Criticism of hollow obligation language can help even a reader who rejects her historical or theological account.
Contemporary test extended: Ask for a reason that justifies the act, then check whether it merely repeats a favorable description of the agent’s purpose.

sections.heading: Read the examples before assigning a moral label
paragraphs: Begin with the opening sections of Intention, following the use of “Why?” rather than looking for a one-sentence definition. Then study the pumping example in sections 23–26 and the shopping-list contrast in section 32. For each description, record what the person knows, what is being pursued and what would count as a mistake.

Read “Modern Moral Philosophy” next, separating its arguments about moral psychology, obligation language and consequentialism. Acceptance of one is not automatic acceptance of the others. Keep the proposal to study justice and flourishing beside the historical claim about law; otherwise the essay can be misread as saying that all ethical thought requires a divine command.

Finally, return to a modest everyday example: intentionally sending a document while accidentally sending an outdated version. Explain both the intentional act and the error without pretending that either description cancels the other. This editorial exercise tests the method before carrying it into harder moral cases.
listItems: Best entry point: Ask what someone is doing and which further purpose makes that description intelligible.
What to watch: Track how the answer changes when the agent lacks knowledge of a consequence or of an aspect of the act.
Where to go next: Compare accounts of practical knowledge, virtue and consequentialism while keeping their distinct questions visible.
Reading discipline: Use the numbered sections of Intention to follow the developing examples, not a detached collection of quotations.
Avoid the shortcut: A good intention is neither the entire action nor a guarantee that the action is justified.

synthesisParagraphs: Anscombe’s analysis connects an agent’s reasons, knowledge and activity. The same performance can support several true descriptions without being intentional under all of them.
Practical knowledge guides action, and the distinction between means and side effects sharpens moral description. Neither makes a person’s self-description immune to scrutiny.
The remaining task is justification: clear descriptions help us see what needs defending, but do not supply an agreed account of justice or flourishing by themselves.

quiz.question: What can be true of a single action?
options: Every true description must be intentional.
It is intentional only if accompanied by a special sensation.
It can be intentional under one description and unintentional under another.
Only its physical description is meaningful.
explanations: The agent can lack knowledge of one aspect or consequence.
The account rejects intention as mere mental decoration.
Turning a handle knowingly and making an unknown noise illustrate the distinction.
Purpose is part of what an action explanation investigates.

quiz.question: What does the relevant “Why?” question seek?
options: A reason for acting, such as filling a tank.
Only a description of muscle contraction.
Proof that the agent is morally admirable.
A complete explanation of the universe.
explanations: This connects the action with its purpose.
A bodily cause answers a different question.
Explaining a reason does not certify its moral quality.
The question concerns the intelligibility of this activity.

quiz.question: What is distinctive about the shopper’s list?
options: It reports purchases from an observer’s viewpoint.
It cannot be mistaken.
It makes unsuccessful shopping successful by definition.
It guides what is to be bought, whereas the detective’s list records purchases.
explanations: That is the detective’s role in the contrast.
Lists and execution can fail.
Practical guidance does not guarantee success.
The role determines whether a mismatch calls for correcting the shopping or the record.

quiz.question: When is unwanted harm still an intended means?
options: Whenever any harm is foreseeable.
When the agent chooses the harm as the route to the goal.
Only when the agent enjoys it.
Never, if the agent states a good purpose.
explanations: Foreseeability alone does not establish a means.
Disliking a chosen means does not make it a side effect.
Enjoyment is not the criterion.
A good purpose cannot erase the means chosen.

quiz.question: What does the critique of obligation language claim?
options: Nonbelievers are incapable of good conduct.
Every ethical concept is meaningless.
A law-like moral ought needs an account of its authority and sense.
All consequences are irrelevant to every judgment.
explanations: This is not a claim about nonbelievers’ character.
Justice and flourishing remain subjects of inquiry.
The historical diagnosis concerns a particular conception of obligation.
The critique is not a license to ignore consequences.

quiz.question: What does the falsified-report case reveal?
options: An intelligible purpose can coexist with a chosen act needing moral justification.
Protecting jobs removes the deception from the action.
A favorable description settles the case.
An official cannot act intentionally.
explanations: Explaining the purpose leaves the justificatory question open.
The deception remains deliberate.
The description must include what was actually chosen.
Nothing in the case removes intentional agency.

quiz.question: Which question remains after intentions are clear?
options: Whether there was any bodily movement at all.
Whether all people use identical words.
Whether the agent can redescribe the act favorably.
Which account of justice or flourishing justifies the moral judgment.
explanations: Physical details may matter, but this is not the central remaining moral issue.
Agreement in wording need not settle standards.
A favorable description does not provide justification.
The profile keeps disagreement about standards distinct from description.

quiz.question: How should an accidentally outdated attachment be described?
options: As wholly unintentional because one error occurred.
As intentionally sent, though not intentionally outdated if the sender did not know.
As successful simply because the sender intended success.
As proof that all action knowledge is spectator knowledge.
explanations: An error in one respect need not cancel the intended act.
The two descriptions identify different aspects of the same activity.
Intention does not guarantee execution.
The example permits guided action together with error.
